{{Short description|Every rigid motion is a screw displacement}}
{{Other uses|Chasles' theorem (disambiguation)}}

[[Image:pure screw.svg|thumb|A [[screw axis]].  Mozzi–Chasles' theorem says that every [[Euclidean motion]] is a screw displacement along some screw axis.]]In [[kinematics]], '''Chasles' theorem''', or '''Mozzi–Chasles' theorem''', says that the most general [[rigid body displacement]] can be produced by a '''screw displacement''' or '''screw motion'''. A direct [[Euclidean isometry]] in three dimensions involves a [[translation (geometry)|translation]] and a [[rotation]]. The screw displacement representation of the isometry decomposes the translation into two components, one parallel to the [[axis of rotation]] associated with the isometry and the other component perpendicular to that axis. The Chasles theorem states that the axis of rotation can be selected to provide the second component of the original translation as a result of the rotation. This theorem in three dimensions extends a similar representation of planar isometries as rotation. Once the [[screw axis]] is selected, the screw displacement rotates about it and a translation parallel to the axis is included in the screw displacement.<ref>{{cite book | last=Heard | first=William B.| year=2006 | title=Rigid Body Mechanics | publisher=Wiley | page= 42 | isbn=3-527-40620-4}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Joseph|first=Toby|date=2020|title=An Alternative Proof of Euler's Rotation Theorem|url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00283-020-09991-z|journal=The Mathematical Intelligencer|volume=42|issue=4|pages=44–49|language=en|doi=10.1007/s00283-020-09991-z|issn=0343-6993|arxiv=2008.05378|s2cid=221103695}}</ref>

== Planar isometries with complex numbers ==
[[Euclidean geometry]] is expressed in the [[complex plane]] by points <math>p = x + y i</math> where i squared is &minus;1. Rotations result from multiplications by <math>\omega = \cos t + i \sin t </math>.
Note that a rotation about complex point ''p'' is obtained by complex arithmetic with

<math display=block>
z \mapsto \omega (z - p) + p = \omega z + p(1 - \omega)
</math>

where the last expression shows the mapping equivalent to rotation at 0 and a translation.
Therefore, given direct isometry <math>z \mapsto \omega z + a,</math> one can solve <math>p(1 - \omega) = a</math> to obtain <math>p = a/(1 - \omega)</math> as the center for an equivalent rotation, provided that <math>\omega \ne 1</math>, that is, provided the direct isometry is not a pure translation. As stated by Cederberg, "A direct isometry is either a rotation or a translation."<ref>{{cite book| last=Cederberg|first=Judith N.| year=2001| title=A Course in Modern Geometries| url=https://archive.org/details/coursemoderngeom00cede| url-access=limited| pages=[https://archive.org/details/coursemoderngeom00cede/page/n153 136]–164|publisher=Springer | isbn=978-0-387-98972-3}}, quote from page 151</ref>

==History==
The proof that a spatial displacement can be decomposed into a rotation and slide around and along a line is attributed to the astronomer and mathematician {{Ill|Giulio Giuseppe Mozzi|it}} (1763), in fact the screw axis is traditionally called '''asse di Mozzi''' in Italy. However, most textbooks refer to a subsequent similar work by [[Michel Chasles]] dating from 1830.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Chasles | first=M. | year=1830 | title=Note sur les propriétés générales du système de deux corps semblables entr'eux | journal=Bulletin des Sciences Mathématiques, Astronomiques, Physiques et Chemiques | volume=14 | pages=321–326 | language=fr | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ERcAAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA321 }}</ref><!--date given in article is 5 Feb 1831--> Several other contemporaries of M. Chasles obtained the same or similar results around that time, including {{Ill|Gaetano Giorgini|it}}, [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy]], [[Louis Poinsot]], [[Siméon Denis Poisson]] and [[Olinde Rodrigues]].  An account of the 1763 proof by Giulio Mozzi and some of its history can be found here.<ref>
{{cite book | last=Mozzi | first=Giulio | year=1763 | title=Discorso matematico sopra il rotamento momentaneo dei corpi | publisher=Stamperia di Donato Campo | place=Napoli | url=https://archive.org/stream/discorsomatemat00mozzgoog#page/n5/mode/2up | language=it }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last=Ceccarelli  | first=Marco | year=2000 | title=Screw axis defined by Giulio Mozzi in 1763 and early studies on helicoidal motion | journal=Mechanism and Machine Theory | volume=35 | issue=6 | pages=761–770 | doi=10.1016/S0094-114X(99)00046-4 }}</ref>

==Proof==
Mozzi considers a rigid body undergoing first a rotation about an axis passing through the [[center of mass]] and then a translation of displacement D in an arbitrary direction. Any rigid motion can be accomplished in this way due to [[Euler's rotation theorem|a theorem by Euler on the existence of an axis of rotation]]. 
The displacement D of the center of mass can be decomposed into components parallel and perpendicular to the axis. The perpendicular (and parallel) component acts on all points of the rigid body but Mozzi shows that for some points the previous rotation acted exactly with an opposite displacement, so those points are translated parallel to the axis of rotation. These points lie on the Mozzi axis through which the rigid motion can be accomplished through a screw motion.

Another [[elementary proof]] of Mozzi–Chasles' theorem was given by [[E. T. Whittaker]] in 1904.<ref>[[E. T. Whittaker]] (1904) {{cite book|author=E. T. Whittaker|author-link=E. T. Whittaker|title=[[A Treatise on the Analytical Dynamics of Particles and Rigid Bodies]]| page=4}}</ref> Suppose ''A'' is to be transformed into ''B''. Whittaker suggests that line ''AK'' be selected parallel to the axis of the given rotation, with ''K'' the foot of a perpendicular from ''B''. The appropriate screw displacement is about an axis parallel to ''AK'' such that ''K'' is moved to ''B''. In Whittaker's terms, "A rotation about any axis is equivalent to a rotation through the same angle about any axis parallel to it, together with a simple translation in a direction perpendicular to the axis."

== Calculation ==
The calculation of the commuting translation and rotation from a screw motion can be performed using [[Plane-based Geometric Algebra|3DPGA]] (<math>\mathbb{R}_{3,0,1}</math>), the [[geometric algebra]] of 3D Euclidean space.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Gunn|first=Charles|date=2011-12-19|others=Technische Universität Berlin, Technische Universität Berlin, Ulrich Pinkall|title=Geometry, Kinematics, and Rigid Body Mechanics in Cayley-Klein Geometries|language=en|doi=10.14279/DEPOSITONCE-3058|type=Master's thesis}}</ref> It has three Euclidean basis vectors <math>\mathbf{e}_i</math> satisfying <math>\mathbf{e}_i^2 = 1</math> representing orthogonal planes through the origin, and one [[Grassmannian]] basis vector <math>\mathbf{e}_0</math> satisfying <math>\mathbf{e}_0^2 = 0</math> to represent the plane at infinity. Any plane a distance <math>\delta</math> from the origin can then be formed as a [[linear combination]] <math display="block">a = \sum_{i=1}^3 a^i \mathbf{e}_i - \delta \mathbf{e}_0</math>which is normalized such that <math>a^2 = 1</math>. Because reflections can be represented by the plane in which the reflection occurs, the product of two planes <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> is the bireflection <math>ab</math>. The result is a rotation around their intersection line <math>a \wedge b</math>, which could also lie on the plane at infinity when the two reflections are parallel, in which case the bireflection <math>ab</math> is a translation.

A screw motion <math>S</math> is the product of four non-collinear reflections, and thus <math>S = abcd</math>. But according to the Mozzi-Chasles' theorem a screw motion can be decomposed into a commuting translation <math display="block">T = e^{\alpha B_1} = 1 + \alpha B_1</math>where <math>B_1</math> is the axis of translation satisfying <math>B_1^2 = 0</math>, and rotation<math display="block">R = e^{\beta B_2} = \cos(\beta) + B_2 \sin(\beta)</math>where <math>B_2</math> is the axis of rotation satisfying <math>B_2^2 = -1</math>. The two bivector lines <math>B_1</math> and <math>B_2</math> are orthogonal and commuting. To find <math>T</math> and <math>R</math> from <math>S</math>, we simply write out <math>S</math> and consider the result grade-by-grade:<math display="block">\begin{aligned} S &= TR \\
&= e^{\alpha B_1} e^{\beta B_2} \\
&= \underbrace{\cos \beta}_{\text{scalar}} + \underbrace{\sin \beta B_2 + \alpha \cos \beta B_1}_{\text{bivector}} + \underbrace{\alpha \sin \beta B_1 B_2}_\text{quadrivector} 
\end{aligned}</math>Because the quadrivector part <math>\langle S \rangle_4 = \langle T \rangle_2 \langle R \rangle_2 </math> and <math>B_1^2 = 0 </math>, <math>T </math> is directly found to be<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Roelfs|first1=Martin|last2=De Keninck|first2=Steven|title=Graded Symmetry Groups: Plane and Simple|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/353116859}}</ref><math display="block">T = 1 + \frac{\langle S \rangle_4}{\langle S \rangle_2}</math>and thus<math display="block">R = S T^{-1} = T^{-1} S = \frac{S}{T}</math>Thus, for a given screw motion <math>S</math> the commuting translation and rotation can be found using the two formulae above, after which the lines <math>B_1</math> and <math>B_2</math> are found to be proportional to <math>\langle T \rangle_2 </math> and <math>\langle R \rangle_2 </math> respectively.

== Other dimensions and fields ==
The Chasles' theorem is a special case of the [[Invariant decomposition]].
